source: Khandelwal, Rossi et al. (2025) Language Models Coupled with Metacognition Can Outperform Reasoning Models (SOFAI-LM)
finding: A small fast LLM, wrapped in a code-run metacognitive feedback loop, beats a standalone reasoning model. The slow reasoner is called only when the fast loop fails. No training.
numbers: Granite 3.3 8B (no thinking) vs DeepSeek R1 8B. Graph coloring size 25: SOFAI-LM solves 42%, the reasoning model alone 2%. DebugBench: SOFAI-LM Python 70%, C++ 73%; reasoning model alone 37% and 40%, and slower.
limits: Two domains only; 8B models; AAAI 2026 paper. Other model pairs said to be consistent (supplement).
agent_relevance: Direct match to our design: program runs the loop and the budget, model fills slots, slow solver is a fallback.

source: Khandelwal, Rossi et al. (2025) Language Models Coupled with Metacognition Can Outperform Reasoning Models (SOFAI-LM)
finding: More feedback iterations raise success but cost time. Most of the gain comes in the first 5 rounds.
numbers: LLM, LLM@5, LLM@10, LLM@15 tested. Biggest jump between LLM and LLM@5; LLM@15 best but slowest. Reasoning model degrades fast as graph size grows.
limits: Compute time rises with iterations; figures read from plots, no table seen.
agent_relevance: Cap feedback rounds (about 5) and hand off to a slower path after that.

source: Khandelwal, Rossi et al. (2025) Language Models Coupled with Metacognition Can Outperform Reasoning Models (SOFAI-LM)
finding: What to pass to the slow solver depends on the task. For graph coloring, passing past failed attempts hurts. For code debugging, it helps.
numbers: Three LRM prompts: PO (problem only), BA (best attempt), FH (full history). Graph coloring: PO best. Code debugging: BA and FH beat PO but cost more time. Feedback style: multi-line feedback plus minimal memory gave 42% at about 27 s, best of four settings.
quote: Providing negative examples ... is not helpful, and actually detrimental
limits: Authors' explanation (local fix vs global revision) is a conjecture, not tested.
agent_relevance: Passing failed attempts into a retry is not always good. Global-consistency tasks want a clean restart; local-fix tasks want the history. Matches our G-rules on correlated errors.

source: Khandelwal, Pallagani, Srivastava, Rossi (2025) A Neurosymbolic Fast and Slow Architecture for Graph Coloring (SOFAI-v2)
finding: SOFAI-v2 uses an LLM as fast S1, a symbolic solver as slow S2, and a metacognition module that gives targeted feedback and episodic examples, then escalates. It beats the earlier SOFAI-v1 mainly on hard or unsolvable instances.
numbers: Abstract: 10.5% higher success rate and up to 30% faster than a traditional symbolic solver. Graph size 50, unsolvable set: 53.85% vs 3.85% for v1 and S1. Mixed set: 27.72% vs 2.11%. 200 s limit, averaged over 3 runs.
limits: Graph coloring only. Time results (about 14,000 s vs 20,000 s total at n=50) were measured with no time limit and compared with v1 and S2, not S1.
agent_relevance: Escalation rule plus memory of past instances is what helps hard cases; a plain fast-then-slow router does not.

source: Khandelwal, Pallagani, Srivastava, Rossi (2025) A Neurosymbolic Fast and Slow Architecture for Graph Coloring (SOFAI-v2)
finding: Repeated S1 calls with structured feedback raise success steadily.
numbers: Solvable set n=5: about 20% at iteration 1 to nearly 80% at iteration 5. Unsolvable n=10: about 60% to 85%. Mixed n=10: about 40% to 60%.
limits: Values read from plots (approximate).
agent_relevance: Supports iterative checked retries with a hard cap before escalation.

source: Fabiano, Pallagani, Ganapini, et al. (2023) Fast and Slow Planning
finding: Plan-SOFAI: a case-based or Plansformer fast solver plus classical or epistemic planners as slow solver, governed by a metacognitive module. Experience lets fast solver take over repeat problems.
numbers: 700 classical instances: Mix and Plansformer configs solved 671; random-memory baseline 587; Jaccard 593; Mix about 19% faster than Fast Downward. Epistemic planning: EFP 2.0 solved 149 vs Jaccard S1 222, 49% faster.
limits: Fast Downward wins on easy problems; accepts partial plans (correctness over 0.5). The Fast Downward cell in the table was garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Experience-based fast path plus slow planner is a cheap hybrid; partial answers can beat none.

source: Ganapini, Campbell, Fabiano, et al. (2021) Thinking Fast and Slow in AI: the Role of Metacognition
finding: Original SOFAI proposal. S1 solvers use only past experience, S2 solvers are triggered by need. A metacognitive agent arbitrates using resources, solver skill, past experience and expected reward, in two phases (fast approximate, then careful).
numbers: No experiments in this document; two instances in progress.
limits: Position paper. Later work (SOFAI-v2, SOFAI-LM) supplies the numbers.
agent_relevance: Explicit arbitration rule as code, in two cheap-then-careful phases.

source: Sun (2025) Enhancing Computational Cognitive Architectures with LLMs: A Case Study (CLARION + LLMs)
finding: Sun proposes putting fine-tuned LLMs at the implicit (bottom) level of CLARION and keeping explicit rules on top. LLMs cover language, perception, motor, memory and intuition. Explicit rules direct the LLM and do precise reasoning and planning in new situations.
numbers: No experiments or numbers. Sun argues LLM limits on symbolic reasoning are what human implicit processes show.
limits: Conceptual paper. Claim that good LLM reasoning is still 'intuition' is argued, not measured.
agent_relevance: Gives the role split we want: model as implicit layer, code-run explicit rules and checks on top.

source: Sun (2025) Enhancing Computational Cognitive Architectures with LLMs: A Case Study (CLARION + LLMs)
finding: Two-way learning in CLARION carries over: bottom-up (implicit to explicit rules, by information gain) and top-down (explicit rules assimilated into implicit nets).
numbers: Not quantified here.
limits: Under LLMs, bottom-up extraction needs a success signal that is often missing.
agent_relevance: Candidate method: extract rules from successful model outputs and re-inject them as checked scaffolds.

source: Sun (2024) Can A Cognitive Architecture Fundamentally Enhance LLMs? Or Vice Versa?
finding: Argues LLMs act roughly like implicit processes (intuition) and need an explicit symbolic and metacognitive side for reliability. Also says cognitive architectures need overhaul to use modern AI.
numbers: No experiments. Cites others claiming GPT-4 captures fast but not slow thinking.
limits: Position paper from the CLARION author; not independent.
agent_relevance: Frames our scaffold as the explicit layer around an implicit model.

source: Sun (2005) Slides: From Hybrid Systems to Hybrid Cognitive Architectures (CLARION overview)
finding: List of human data sets CLARION has been fitted to, with focus on the synergy of implicit and explicit learning, mainly via bottom-up learning.
numbers: Tasks: process control (Berry and Broadbent 1988; Stanley 1989; Dienes and Fahey 1995), serial reaction time (Lewicki 1987; Curran and Keele 1993), artificial grammar (Domangue 2004), letter counting (Rabinowitz and Goldberg 1995), Tower of Hanoi, minefield navigation, metacognitive monitoring.
limits: Slides, not a paper; numbers and fit statistics not given. Fits are by the model's own authors. URL is a pointer to the author's page, not the exact slide file.
agent_relevance: Background only: human data side is covered by angles A and B.

source: Romero, Zimmerman, Steinfeld, Tomasic (2023) Synergistic Integration of LLMs and Cognitive Architectures for Robust AI
finding: Three integration routes: modular, agency, and a CLARION-style neuro-symbolic one. In the CLARION-style one, bottom-up learning turns LLM outputs into symbolic rules, top-down guidance puts rules into prompts.
numbers: Example: user instruction becomes an independent rule; a successful LLM answer becomes an extracted rule that is generalised (add values) or specialised (remove values or add dimensions). Rule choice by information gain or Boltzmann over utility.
limits: Exploratory; 'preliminary evidence' is ChatGPT examples, no benchmark scores.
agent_relevance: Concrete design: generalise and specialise rules based on outcomes; a metacognitive module sets probabilities of using each level.

source: Romero, Zimmerman, Steinfeld, Tomasic (2023) Synergistic Integration of LLMs and Cognitive Architectures for Robust AI
finding: Tight LLM and architecture coupling inherits LLM failures. Authors note cascading errors from hallucination and bias when the LLM generates productions or simulated futures.
numbers: Case: ChatGPT prompted to write ACT-R productions; no accuracy measure.
limits: Anecdotal.
agent_relevance: Keep checks in code, not inside model-generated rules.

source: Lin, Fu, Yang, et al. (2023) SwiftSage: A Generative Agent with Fast and Slow Thinking
finding: Fast small fine-tuned seq2seq model acts by default; GPT-4 plans subgoals and grounds actions when a heuristic says the fast model is stuck.
numbers: ScienceWorld, 30 task types: SwiftSage 84.7 average; SayCan 33.8; ReAct 36.4; Reflexion 45.3. Uses far fewer LLM tokens per action.
limits: Fast module needs behavior cloning on oracle trajectories; one benchmark; GPT-4 only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a cheap fast path plus rare slow calls beats calling the big model each step.

source: Yu, Xu, Weston, Kulikov (2024) Distilling System 2 into System 1
finding: Fine-tuning a model on its own filtered slow-reasoning outputs can move the skill into direct answers, but not for every task.
numbers: Llama-2-70B-chat: last-letter concat 30.0% zero-shot, 39.5% System 2, 98.0% distilled 2-Step RaR. Coin flip 56.1% to 75.69% distilled. Math (GSM8K): System 1 about 9.4%, System 2 52.77%, distilled CoT 7.13% (fails).
limits: Needs training, so outside our no-training rule; CoT distillation failed on math.
agent_relevance: Shows which slow steps could become fast habits; for us it only informs which steps are worth caching as templates.

source: Christakopoulou, Mourad, Mataric (2024) Agents Thinking Fast and Slow: A Talker-Reasoner Architecture
finding: Talker answers with low latency from the last stored belief; Reasoner does multi-step planning and updates a shared belief in memory. The two can be out of sync.
numbers: Sleep-coaching case study; text read gave qualitative dialogue examples, no benchmark scores found.
limits: No numbers seen; Talker may use outdated beliefs.
agent_relevance: A shared explicit belief store between fast and slow parts.

source: Zhang, Wang, et al. (2025) Leveraging Dual Process Theory in Language Agent Framework (DPT-Agent)
finding: Real-time collaboration (Overcooked) needs both parts: code-as-policy finite-state machine as System 1, LLM Theory of Mind plus asynchronous reflection as System 2. Independent S1 or S2 alone fails on latency or score.
numbers: Rule-based partner, GPT-4o: ReAct 7.00, Reflexion 4.83, DPT variants 56.50 and 51.33 (column order not verified). Llama3.3-70b ReAct 15.50, Reflexion -43.33. Human study N=71: Map 1 mean score ReAct 99.03, Reflexion 97.78, DPT w/o ToM 103.19, DPT 111.53; Map 2 115.00, 119.67, 152.03, 160.63.
limits: Real-time game; ToM module did not always help (Map 2 humans preferred the version without it).
agent_relevance: Fast scripted layer plus slow reasoner helps when latency matters; not our use case, so background.

source: Ustun, Rosenbloom, Sajjadi, Nuttall (2018) Controlling Synthetic Characters in Simulations: A Case for Cognitive Architectures and Sigma
finding: Sigma builds every capability on factor graphs with summary-product message passing and gradient-descent learning, so symbolic, probabilistic, neural and reinforcement learning share one base.
numbers: Frozen-lake style test: reinforcement learner augmented with learned action model and hole locations reached goal 79% of test runs.
limits: Small toy tasks; no comparison to LLM agents; applied to simulated characters.
agent_relevance: Sigma has no LLM tests that we found; its value to us is the idea of one uniform mechanism, which our schema deliberately does not copy (we keep code and model separate).

source: Rosenbloom, Demski, Ustun (2016-2017) Sigma neural extensions (cited in Ustun 2018)
finding: Cited only: Sigma was extended to neural networks in two AGI conference papers. Not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Not read this session.
agent_relevance: Pointer for later.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) Position: LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks
finding: LLM generates, external sound verifiers critique, loop repeats. LLMs cannot reliably self-verify.
numbers: Reported: GPT-4 plans executable about 12% on average; with VAL back-prompting Blocks World reaches 82% in 15 rounds, Logistics 70%, obfuscated Mystery Blocks World only about 10%.
limits: Gains depend on an external checker; obfuscated domain barely improves.
agent_relevance: Strong support for code-run checks over self-judgment (G rules).

source: Hagendorff (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Older GPT-3 models answer cognitive reflection and semantic-illusion tasks intuitively (System 1-like), more than humans. ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 switch to chain-of-thought and mostly stop.
numbers: Intuitive wrong answers: GPT-3 davinci family 70-90% vs humans 55%. Correct: GPT-3 davinci-003 5%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%, humans 38%. Telling davinci-003 to reason step by step raised chain-of-thought responses from 0% to 100%; blocking it in ChatGPT dropped them from 97% to 0.
limits: Tasks may be in training data; models differ in training, not only prompt.
agent_relevance: Chain-of-thought acts as the System 2 switch in models; scaffolds can force or block it.

source: Pan, Albalak, Wang, Wang (2023) Logic-LM
finding: LLM translates the problem into logic; a symbolic solver reasons; self-refinement fixes errors. A neuro-symbolic hybrid in Sun's sense.
numbers: Average +39.2% over standard prompting and +18.4% over chain-of-thought. GPT-4 LogicalDeduction: standard 71.33, CoT 75.25, Logic-LM 87.63. AR-LSAT GPT-4: 33.33, 35.06, 43.04.
limits: Unexecutable translations count as failures; five datasets only.
agent_relevance: Offloading exact reasoning to a solver gives bigger gains than prompting tricks.

source: Khandelwal et al. (2025) SOFAI-v2 graph coloring, edge-probability sweep
finding: Across graph edge densities, the hybrid keeps a lead over each part alone.
numbers: At one setting SOFAI-v2 reached about 94% success vs SOFAI-v1 74%, S1 68%, S2 51%; lead stays 10-20% as edge probability rises; about 72% at p=0.1, 15-25% above the others.
limits: Figures from text; one problem family.
agent_relevance: The combination beats both the fast and slow parts alone, so the router and feedback matter, not only the components.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM execution rates
finding: The hybrid depends on the LLM translating into the formal language correctly. When the solver cannot run, the case fails or falls back.
numbers: ProntoQA execution rate 99.4% (GPT-3.5) and 100% (GPT-4); FOLIO with self-refinement 84.3% accuracy (GPT-3.5) vs 66.7% without.
limits: Numbers from table rows as extracted; FOLIO columns partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Add a code check that the formal form runs, then repair; this is the bottom-up and top-down hand-off in practice.

source: Hagendorff (2023) Semantic illusions and human baselines
finding: On semantic illusions, GPT-3 style models responded intuitively more than people in the comparison study.
numbers: Humans 64% intuitive in the author sample vs 52% in the original study (n=61); CRT 38% correct vs 41% in the original human study (n=3,428).
limits: Human baselines are from other studies; model results are single-prompt tests.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a model's first fluent answer on trap questions; require a deliberate pass.
